Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-22
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Ava Martinez (Redwood AE), Liam Chen (Redwood SE), Maya Thompson (Sierra Prod), Jamal Ortiz (Sierra Platform), Priya Rao (Sierra Security), Connor Lee (Sierra CTO)

Summary:
Quick hosted API demo focused on chat/text generation basics: streaming, common params (temperature, max_tokens, top_p), retry patterns and idempotency, brief Console walkthrough for request examples, and Optimize suggestions (batching, caching) for cost/latency. Customer is evaluating for a payments product assistant with real-time responses and strict security requirements. Next steps agreed (send pricing, SOC2, schedule POC).

Topics covered:
- Intro + qualification (stack, latency targets, timeline)
- Hosted API basics: endpoints, keys, quotas
- Streaming responses and partial token delivery
- Key generation parameters and recommended defaults
- Retries, idempotency tokens, and error handling best practices
- Console quick tour: request inspector, streaming demo, logs
- Redwood Optimize notes: batching, prefix caching, quantization suggestions (high level)
- Compliance ask: SOC2, data retention, VPC/private options

Transcript:
00:00 Ava: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Ava with Redwood Inference, this is Liam our solutions engineer - we'll run through a quick hosted API walkthrough today, wanted to confirm folks can hear me?
00:07 Maya: Yep, loud and clear.
00:10 Connor: Good here.
00:15 Ava: Great. quick agenda: 20min demo of chat/text gen, streaming + params, then 10-ish min on retries and error handling and a short Console tour. Save Qs for after or ping in chat.
00:30 Liam: I'll kick off with the API basics then show a live stream example, FYI the demo uses a small test model; performance in prod will vary by pinned model and region.
00:45 Maya: Quick qual - current stack, we're on GCP, microservices in k8s. Latency target is sub-300ms for short messages, and we need high throughput during peaks. Also security - we can't send PII off-shore.
01:05 Liam: Ok, good to know. hosted API supports region selection and data controls; for strict residency you can run Redwood Private or use dedicated capacity, but hosted can be region pinned in many cases. For the demo we'll show streaming from the hosted endpoint and the Console.
01:25 Jamal: What's your rate limiting model? We expect bursty traffic from 100 to 3k reqs/min per service.
01:37 Ava: For hosted API we expose quota configs per account, and rate limits per key. If you need predictable throughput we often recommend Dedicated pools. We can also implement token bucket policies per route.
01:50 Liam: Ok moving to the code, here's the simple chat call - request includes model, messages, temperature, max_tokens. We'll show streaming (server-sent events) so you can render partial tokens in the UI.
02:05 [screen share starts]
02:10 Liam: Alright I'm calling the /v1/chat/completions endpoint; first non-stream: you get the full response once done, but with stream=true you'll get incremental chunks with delta tokens. This reduces TTFB for UI rendering.
02:30 Liam: Live stream example now - curl with -N, we open socket and you see tokens arrive every ~50-200ms depending on model and backend batching.
02:48 Maya: So stream reduces latency because you don't wait for the whole answer, right?
02:55 Liam: Exactly. You render partial tokens; note that streaming doesn't change total compute much but improves perceived latency. Also careful with UI: need to handle partial sentences and finalization events.
03:10 Liam: One thing to watch is retries: if a streaming connection breaks, you can resume with an idempotency token and a cursor or simply re-ask but dedupe on your side. We recommend short-lived idempotency keys for non-idempotent calls and to use request IDs for at-least-once semantics.
03:30 Jamal: Do you have automatic resume or is it client-side?
03:35 Liam: Currently client-side. We provide SDK helpers that simplify reconnect + replay of messages; for more advanced resume we suggest storing last confirmed token indices in the UI.
03:48 Ava: Also worth calling out parameters: temperature controls randomness, top_p is nucleus sampling; for deterministic responses set temp=0 and top_p=1. max_tokens caps completion length. We include token cost in the response headers so you can estimate spend.
04:05 Maya: What's the retry policy for 5xx vs rate limit 429?
04:12 Liam: For 5xx we recommend exponential backoff with jitter, for 429 we recommend honoring Retry-After if provided and exponential backoff; also consider client side queueing or a leaky-bucket to smooth bursts. We can provide sample code.
04:30 Ava: We'll share our recommended retry snippet - it includes idempotency token generation and backoff strategy.
04:40 Liam: Quick demo of the Console - request inspector shows payload, timing, and per-token breakdown. You can toggle stream in the Console and watch partial token flow. It also surfaces latency percentiles by model version.
05:05 [Console demo - small pause while switching tabs]
05:20 Liam: In the Console logs you can see trace IDs; those map to request ids returned by the API so you can correlate traces with Redwood's tracing. Helpful during debugging or when you open a support ticket.
05:35 Priya: Security question - for hosted, do you persist the request/response content? We need strict rules on retention and redaction.
05:42 Ava: By default hosted keeps logs for X days (we'll insert exact retention in the SOC2 doc), but for sensitive workloads we recommend Dedicated or Private where you control retention and KMS. We also offer field-level redaction options and audit logs.
06:00 Priya: And KMS? customer-managed keys?
06:04 Ava: Yes, for Dedicated and Private you can integrate with your KMS/HSM; hosted has tenant encryption at rest and we do manage keys, but we provide options for bring-your-own-key for higher tiers.
06:20 Connor: On cost - how much can Optimize reduce per-token cost?
06:26 Liam: Typical wins come from batching, prefix/KV caching and model-quantization choices; for chat-heavy workloads prefix caching can reduce repeated tokens significantly. We usually see 20-50% improvements depending on workload. We'll run a cost simulation during the POC.
06:45 Maya: For POC we'll want a benchmarking window and a representative dataset. Our success metric is 95th perc latency < 300ms and cost per request under $0.02.
07:00 Ava: That sounds reasonable - we'll include those SLAs in the POC scope doc.
07:10 Liam: Back to streaming: small demo of param tuning - lowering temperature and setting max_tokens to smaller values to cap cost. Also you can use stop sequences to end generation early.
07:30 [demo continues, Liam types code]
07:50 Liam: Also discuss retries for streaming: if connection fails mid-stream, clients can reconnect and fetch messages since last ack if they maintain a cursor. For most customers a simple reconnect + server-side duplicate suppression is fine.
08:15 Jamal: Anything special for k8s-based clients? We have autoscaling and short-lived pods.
08:23 Liam: For ephemeral pods we recommend lightweight SDK usage and avoid long-lived streaming from many pods concurrently; use a proxy or aggregator to multiplex streams. Batching at the proxy can reduce cost and smooth traffic.
08:40 Maya: Can you show SDK examples?
08:45 Liam: Sure - here's a python snippet and a node snippet. Node streaming uses eventsource polyfill, python uses SSE client or websockets depending on SDK. We'll attach those examples.
09:05 Ava: On quotas and keys, you can rotate keys via the Console, set per-route quotas, and create service keys limited to embeddings or chat only.
09:20 Priya: Audit logs - do you provide SSO/SCIM or RBAC?
09:24 Ava: Yes SSO/SAML and SCIM provisioning, RBAC controls for roles and route permissions; we'll include our security matrix in the doc pack.
09:40 Liam: Quick note on error codes: 400s are client errors, 401 for auth, 403 for permissions, 404 for endpoints, 409 for conflicting operations; 429 rate limiting, 5xx server errors. We recommend handling each class differently in the client.
10:05 Maya: For our payments assistant we also want function/tool calling - is that supported?
10:12 Liam: Yes, we support structured output and tool calling via the chat schema (function signatures). You can register tools and Redwood will surface the structured response. It's supported in hosted API.
10:30 Ava: We're about halfway through demo - any burning questions?
10:35 Jamal: One more on streaming: latency numbers - do you have real metrics?
10:38 Liam: We publish benchmark profiles per model in the catalog; for small prompts some models can start streaming tokens within 50-120ms depending on region and load. We'll share the profile sheet.
10:55 [brief silence; participants reviewing]
11:10 Liam: Now a quick look at Optimize - in the Console we surface batching suggestions and quantization flags for models; also a safety net for quality regression alerts tied to eval prompt sets. For chat if you have repetitive system messages we recommend prefix caching.
11:35 Maya: Is prefix caching safe with PII?
11:40 Ava: For PII we advise not caching or use field-level redaction before caching. If you need full control use Private where caching lives in your VPC.
11:55 Liam: We also have a reranking endpoint and embeddings; rerank can help boost answer quality if you have a retrieval step.
12:15 Maya: Ok great. let's recap next steps.
12:20 Ava: Recap - we'll send pricing, SOC2 and retention, streaming + retry code samples, and proposed POC plan. Sierra to confirm POC dataset and timeline.
12:35 Connor: Sounds good, want to get the POC scheduled next week Tue or Wed morning PST.
12:40 Maya: Tue works.
12:45 Ava: I'll follow up with a calendar invite and an initial POC scope doc.
12:50 [meeting ends]
